paragraphs: Besides the defects already listed in the existing federal system, there are others of equal importance, and together they make it altogether unfit for managing the affairs of the Union.

All parties admit that the lack of a power to regulate commerce is one of these. I anticipated the usefulness of such a power under the first head of our inquiries, and for that reason, and because everyone is convinced of it, little needs to be added here. Even at the most superficial glance it is evident that no object, whether for the interests of trade or of finance, more strongly calls for federal oversight. The lack of it has already blocked the making of beneficial treaties with foreign powers and has caused dissatisfaction among the States. No nation that understands the nature of our political association would be foolish enough to make agreements with the United States in which it gave up privileges of any importance to itself, when it knew that the Union's commitments could be broken at any moment by its members, and when experience showed that it could enjoy every advantage it wanted in our markets without granting us anything in return except what its momentary convenience might suggest. It is no wonder, then, that Mr. Jenkinson, when he brought into the House of Commons a bill to regulate the temporary dealings between the two countries, began by declaring that similar provisions in earlier bills had served every purpose for the commerce of Great Britain, and that it would be prudent to stay with the plan until it became clear whether the American government was likely to gain greater stability.(1)

Several States have tried, through separate prohibitions, restrictions, and exclusions, to influence the conduct of that kingdom in this respect. But the lack of concert, which comes from the lack of a general authority and from the clashing and dissimilar views of the States, has so far defeated every such experiment, and will keep defeating them as long as the same obstacles to uniform measures remain.

The meddling and unneighborly regulations of some States, contrary to the true spirit of the Union, have in different instances given other States just cause for offense and complaint. It is to be feared that if a national control does not restrain such examples, they will multiply and spread until they become as serious a source of animosity and discord as they are a harmful obstacle to trade between the different parts of the Confederacy. "The commerce of the German empire(2) is in continual trammels from the multiplicity of the duties which the several princes and states exact upon the merchandises passing through their territories, by means of which the fine streams and navigable rivers with which Germany is so happily watered are rendered almost useless." The character of the people of this country might never allow this description to apply to us strictly. Still, from the gradual clashes of State regulations we may reasonably expect that the citizens of each State would in the end come to be regarded and treated by the others as no better than foreigners and aliens.

On the plainest reading of the articles of the Confederation, the power of raising armies is merely a power to make requisitions on the States for quotas of men. In the recent war, this practice was found full of obstacles to a vigorous and economical system of defense. It gave rise to a competition among the States that turned into a kind of auction for men. To supply the quotas required of them, they outbid each other until the bounties grew to an enormous and unsupportable size. The hope that they would rise still further gave those inclined to serve a reason to put off enlisting, and made them unwilling to sign on for any considerable period. The results were slow and scanty levies of men in the most critical emergencies of our affairs; short enlistments at an unparalleled expense; and continual shifts in the troops, which ruined their discipline and often exposed the public safety to the perilous crisis of a disbanded army. Hence also came the oppressive expedients for raising men that were used on several occasions, and which nothing but enthusiasm for liberty would have led the people to endure.

This method of raising troops is no more friendly to economy and vigor than it is to an equal distribution of the burden. The States near the seat of war, moved by the need to preserve themselves, made efforts to supply their quotas that even exceeded their abilities, while those far from danger were for the most part as slack in their exertions as the others were diligent. In this case, unlike the case of money contributions, the immediate weight of this inequality was not eased by the hope of a final settling of accounts. The States that did not pay their share of money could at least be charged with their deficiencies, but no account could be made of the deficiencies in the supply of men. We shall not see much reason to regret the lack of that hope, however, when we consider how little prospect there is that the most delinquent States will ever be able to make up their failures in money. The system of quotas and requisitions, whether applied to men or to money, is in every view a system of weakness in the Union and of inequality and injustice among the members.

The right of equal suffrage among the States is another objectionable part of the Confederation. Every idea of proportion and every rule of fair representation condemns a principle that gives Rhode Island equal weight in the scale of power with Massachusetts, Connecticut, or New York, and gives Delaware an equal voice in the national deliberations with Pennsylvania, Virginia, or North Carolina. In its operation it contradicts the fundamental maxim of republican government, which requires that the sense of the majority should prevail. Sophistry may reply that sovereigns are equal, and that a majority of the votes of the States will be a majority of confederated America. But this kind of logical sleight of hand will never overcome the plain suggestions of justice and common sense. It may happen that this majority of States is a small minority of the people of America;(3) and two thirds of the people of America could not long be persuaded, on the strength of artificial distinctions and syllogistic subtleties, to submit their interests to the management and disposal of one third. The larger States would after a while revolt against receiving the law from the smaller. To accept such a deprivation of their due importance in the political scale would be not merely to be insensible to the love of power but even to give up the desire for equality. It is neither reasonable to expect the first nor just to require the last. The smaller States, considering how peculiarly their safety and welfare depend on union, ought readily to give up a pretension that, if it is not relinquished, would prove fatal to the Union's survival.

It may be objected that the most important resolutions need the consent not of seven but of nine States, or two thirds of the whole number, and from this it may be inferred that nine States would always include a majority of the Union. But this does not remove the impropriety of an equal vote between States of the most unequal size and population. Nor is the inference accurate as a matter of fact, for we can name nine States that contain less than a majority of the people;(4) and it is constitutionally possible for these nine to carry the vote. Besides, there are matters of considerable moment that a bare majority can decide, and there are others, about which doubts have been raised, that would reach interests of the first magnitude if they were interpreted in favor of the sufficiency of a vote of seven States. In addition, the number of States will probably increase, and no provision has been made for a proportional increase in the ratio of votes.

But this is not all. What at first sight may seem a remedy is in reality a poison. To give a minority a negative on the majority (which is always the case where more than a majority is required for a decision) is in its tendency to subject the sense of the greater number to that of the lesser. Because a few States failed to attend, Congress has often been in the situation of a Polish diet, where a single VOTE has been enough to stop all its movements. A sixtieth part of the Union, which is about the proportion of Delaware and Rhode Island, has several times been able to put a complete bar on its operations. This is one of those refinements that in practice has an effect the reverse of what theory expects of it. The demand for unanimity in public bodies, or for something approaching it, rests on the supposition that it would add to security. But what it really does is to embarrass the administration, to destroy the energy of the government, and to put the pleasure, caprice, or artifices of an insignificant, turbulent, or corrupt junto in place of the regular deliberations and decisions of a respectable majority. In those emergencies of a nation when the goodness or badness, the weakness or strength, of its government matters most, there is commonly a necessity for action. The public business must go forward in some way. If a stubborn minority can control the opinion of a majority about the best way to conduct it, then the majority, in order that something may be done, must conform to the views of the minority. In this way the sense of the smaller number will overrule that of the greater and set the tone of the national proceedings. The result is tedious delays, continual negotiation and intrigue, and contemptible compromises of the public good. And yet in such a system it is even fortunate when such compromises can be made, for on some occasions things will not allow of accommodation, and then the measures of government must be harmfully suspended or fatally defeated. Often the government is kept in a state of inaction by the impossibility of obtaining the agreement of the necessary number of votes. Its situation must always savor of weakness and sometimes border on anarchy.

It is not hard to see that a principle of this kind gives more scope to foreign corruption, as well as to domestic faction, than the principle that lets the sense of the majority decide, though the opposite has been assumed. The mistake has come from not paying due attention to the harms that may result from obstructing the progress of government at certain critical times. When the Constitution requires the agreement of a large number for any national act, we tend to rest satisfied that all is safe, because nothing improper is likely TO BE DONE. But we forget how much good may be prevented, and how much ill may be produced, by the power to hinder the doing of what may be necessary, and to keep affairs in the same unfavorable position in which they happen to stand at particular times.

Suppose, for instance, that we were at war, together with one foreign nation, against another. Suppose the necessity of our situation called for peace, and the interest or ambition of our ally led him to want to continue the war, with aims that might justify us in making separate terms. In such a situation, this ally of ours would plainly find it much easier, by his bribes and intrigues, to keep the government from making peace where two thirds of all the votes were required for that purpose than where a simple majority would be enough. In the first case he would have to corrupt a smaller number, and in the other a greater. On the same principle, it would be much easier for a foreign power with which we were at war to confuse our councils and hinder our exertions. And in matters of trade we may suffer similar problems. A nation with which we might have a commercial treaty could much more easily prevent our forming a connection with her competitor in trade, even if such a connection would be ever so beneficial to ourselves.

Evils of this kind should not be regarded as imaginary. One of the weak sides of republics, among their many advantages, is that they open too easy an entrance to foreign corruption. A hereditary monarch, though often willing to sacrifice his subjects to his ambition, has so great a personal stake in the government and in the nation's glory abroad that it is not easy for a foreign power to offer him an equivalent for what he would give up by betraying the state. The world has accordingly seen few examples of this kind of royal prostitution, though it has seen plenty of every other kind.

In republics, persons raised from the mass of the community by the votes of their fellow-citizens to positions of great eminence and power may find rewards for betraying their trust. To any but minds animated and guided by superior virtue, these rewards may seem to exceed the share of interest they have in the common stock and to outweigh the obligations of duty. This is why history gives us so many humiliating examples of the prevalence of foreign corruption in republican governments. How much this contributed to the ruin of the ancient commonwealths has already been described. It is well known that the deputies of the United Provinces have in various instances been bought by the emissaries of neighboring kingdoms. The Earl of Chesterfield (if my memory serves me right), in a letter to his court, hinted that the success of an important negotiation depended on his obtaining a major's commission for one of those deputies. And in Sweden the parties were bought in turn by France and England so openly and notoriously that it aroused universal disgust in the nation. It was a principal cause of the transformation, in a single day, without tumult, violence, or opposition, of the most limited monarchy in Europe into one of the most absolute and uncontrolled.

One circumstance that crowns the defects of the Confederation remains to be mentioned: the lack of a judicial power. Laws are a dead letter without courts to explain and define their true meaning and operation. The treaties of the United States, to have any force at all, must be considered part of the law of the land. Their true meaning, so far as individuals are concerned, must be settled, like all other laws, by judicial decisions. To make these decisions uniform, they ought to be submitted, in the last resort, to one SUPREME COURT. And this court ought to be established under the same authority that makes the treaties themselves. Both of these ingredients are indispensable. If each State has a court of final jurisdiction, there may be as many different final decisions on the same point as there are courts. Men's opinions differ endlessly. We often see not only different courts but the judges of the same court disagreeing with each other. To avoid the confusion that would inevitably follow from the contradictory decisions of a number of independent courts, all nations have found it necessary to establish one court above the rest, with general oversight, and with authority to settle and declare in the last resort a uniform rule of civil justice.

This is the more necessary where the frame of the government is so compounded that the laws of the whole are in danger of being violated by the laws of the parts. In that case, if the individual courts are given a right of final jurisdiction, then besides the contradictions to be expected from differences of opinion, there will be much to fear from the bias of local views and prejudices and from the interference of local regulations. Each time such interference occurred, there would be reason to fear that the provisions of the particular laws might be preferred to those of the general laws, for nothing is more natural to men in office than to look with special deference to the authority to which they owe their official existence.

Under the present Constitution, the treaties of the United States are open to violation by thirteen different legislatures and as many different courts of final jurisdiction acting under those legislatures' authority. The good faith, the reputation, and the peace of the whole Union are thus continually at the mercy of the prejudices, passions, and interests of each member of which it is composed. Can foreign nations possibly respect or trust such a government? Can the people of America possibly consent any longer to trust their honor, their happiness, and their safety to so precarious a foundation?

In this review of the Confederation I have confined myself to showing its most material defects. I have passed over the imperfections in its details, through which even a great part of the power meant to be conferred on it has been largely nullified. By this time it must be evident to all thoughtful men who can rid themselves of the prepossessions of preconceived opinions that it is a system so radically vicious and unsound that it admits of no amendment short of an entire change in its leading features and character.

The organization of Congress is itself utterly unsuited to exercising the powers that must be placed in the Union. A single assembly may be a proper holder for the slender, or rather fettered, authorities that have so far been delegated to the federal head. But it would contradict all the principles of good government to entrust it with the additional powers that even the moderate and more reasonable opponents of the proposed Constitution admit ought to reside in the United States. Suppose that plan is not adopted, and suppose the necessity of the Union can withstand the ambitious aims of those who may entertain grand schemes of personal aggrandizement from its dissolution. The probability would then be that we should fall upon the project of giving supplementary powers to Congress as it is now constituted. Then one of two things would happen. Either the machine, from the inherent feebleness of its structure, will crumble to pieces in spite of our ill-judged efforts to prop it up; or, by successive increases of its force and energy as necessity may prompt, we shall finally gather into a single body all the most important prerogatives of sovereignty, and so leave our posterity one of the most execrable forms of government that human folly ever contrived. We should thus create in reality the very tyranny that the opponents of the new Constitution either are, or pretend to be, anxious to avert.

It has contributed not a little to the infirmities of the existing federal system that it was never ratified by the PEOPLE. Resting on no better foundation than the consent of the individual legislatures, it has been exposed to frequent and intricate questions about the validity of its powers, and in some instances it has given birth to the enormous doctrine of a right of legislative repeal. Since it owes its ratification to the law of a State, it has been argued that the same authority might repeal the law by which it was ratified. It is a gross heresy to maintain that a PARTY to a COMPACT has a right to revoke that COMPACT, yet the doctrine has had respectable advocates. The mere possibility of a question of this kind proves the need to lay the foundations of our national government deeper than the mere sanction of delegated authority. The fabric of American empire ought to rest on the solid basis of THE CONSENT OF THE PEOPLE. The streams of national power ought to flow directly from that pure, original fountain of all legitimate authority.
